learner_notice: Commit one response before feedback appears.

items.title: Mobility: Starting check
items.prompt: A pharmacist’s parent worked in a lower-status service occupation. Which classification best fits the across-generation rise in rank?
options: Intergenerational vertical mobility
Intergenerational horizontal mobility
Intragenerational vertical mobility
Intragenerational horizontal mobility
items.directions: Select the best-supported option from the four choices.

items.title: Mobility: Choose with support
items.prompt: During one career, a laboratory technician becomes a supervisor with greater authority and pay. Which classification fits?
options: Intergenerational horizontal mobility
Intragenerational vertical mobility
Intragenerational horizontal mobility
Intergenerational vertical mobility
items.directions: Select the best-supported option from the four choices.

items.title: Mobility: Choose with less support
items.prompt: A physician moves from one hospital to another in a role with similar authority, pay, and prestige. Which classification fits the change?
options: Intergenerational vertical mobility
Intergenerational horizontal mobility
Intragenerational horizontal mobility
Intragenerational vertical mobility
items.directions: Select the best-supported option from the four choices.

items.title: Mobility: Choose independently
items.prompt: A mechanic’s child becomes a mechanic in a different industry with similar income and standing. Which classification fits?
options: Intragenerational vertical mobility
Intergenerational vertical mobility
Intragenerational horizontal mobility
Intergenerational horizontal mobility
items.directions: Select the best-supported option from the four choices.

items.title: Mobility: Near-use check
items.prompt: Over fifteen years, one employee moves from an executive role to a lower-authority assistant role. Which classification best fits?
options: Intragenerational vertical mobility
Intragenerational horizontal mobility
Intergenerational vertical mobility
Intergenerational horizontal mobility
items.directions: Select the best-supported option from the four choices.

items.title: Mobility: Changed-task check
items.prompt: An account says a worker rose because talent and effort are rewarded, but also notes unequal access to training. Which evaluation is best supported?
options: The barrier proves that no individual effort can ever affect mobility
The account invokes meritocracy, but the stated barrier limits the claim
The account describes horizontal mobility because training is unequal
The account proves equal opportunity because the worker advanced
items.directions: Select the best-supported option from the four choices.

items.title: Mobility: Repair the near-use function
items.prompt: After missing a mobility classification, which two questions should be answered before combining labels?
options: High income or low income; absolute poverty or relative poverty
Health outcome or care access; class pattern or race pattern
Across generations or within one life; changed rank or similar rank
Personal effort or shared meaning; exchange cost or social reward
items.directions: Select the best-supported option from the four choices.

items.title: Mobility: Fresh near-use re-entry
items.prompt: A retail worker becomes a similarly ranked warehouse worker during the same decade. Which classification best fits?
options: Intergenerational vertical mobility
Intergenerational horizontal mobility
Intragenerational vertical mobility
Intragenerational horizontal mobility
items.directions: Select the best-supported option from the four choices.

items.title: Mobility: Repair the changed-task function
items.prompt: After missing a meritocracy item, which distinction most directly repairs the evaluation function?
options: Separate an effort-based reward claim from evidence of equal opportunity
Treat every upward movement as proof that all barriers are absent
Classify every job change as horizontal regardless of rank
Replace the mobility account with a detailed threshold calculation
items.directions: Select the best-supported option from the four choices.

items.title: Mobility: Fresh changed-task re-entry
items.prompt: A report credits promotion entirely to effort while noting that only some workers could enter the required program. Which evaluation is best supported?
options: The report proves equal opportunity because one promotion occurred
The report invokes meritocracy, but unequal program access qualifies it
The report describes horizontal mobility because training is involved
The report proves that effort has no relation to any promotion
items.directions: Select the best-supported option from the four choices.

items.title: Poverty and exclusion: Starting check
items.prompt: A household cannot consistently obtain food, safe water, or shelter. Which classification is most directly supported?
options: Relative poverty: resources fall below social norms
Social exclusion: participation is blocked by isolation
Absolute poverty: basic needs cannot be secured
No listed pattern: neither resource nor access gap
items.directions: Select the best-supported option from the four choices.

items.title: Poverty and exclusion: Choose with support
items.prompt: A family has food and shelter but cannot afford routine internet access required for local school and job participation. Which classification best fits the resource comparison?
options: Absolute poverty: basic needs cannot be secured
Social exclusion: participation is blocked by isolation
No listed pattern: neither resource nor access gap
Relative poverty: resources fall below social norms
items.directions: Select the best-supported option from the four choices.

items.title: Poverty and exclusion: Choose with less support
items.prompt: Residents of an isolated district have adequate household income but no transit connection to nearby clinics and schools. Which pattern is most directly described?
options: Social exclusion: participation is blocked by isolation
Relative poverty: resources fall below social norms
Absolute poverty: basic needs cannot be secured
No listed pattern: neither resource nor access gap
items.directions: Select the best-supported option from the four choices.

items.title: Poverty and exclusion: Choose independently
items.prompt: A worker can meet basic needs but has far fewer resources than most neighbors and cannot join ordinary community activities. Which poverty classification fits best?
options: Absolute poverty: basic needs cannot be secured
Relative poverty: resources fall below social norms
No listed pattern: neither resource nor access gap
Social exclusion: participation is blocked by isolation
items.directions: Select the best-supported option from the four choices.

items.title: Poverty and exclusion: Near-use check
items.prompt: A household must regularly skip meals to pay for minimal shelter. Which classification is most directly supported?
options: Relative poverty: resources fall below social norms
No listed pattern: neither resource nor access gap
Absolute poverty: basic needs cannot be secured
Social exclusion: participation is blocked by isolation
items.directions: Select the best-supported option from the four choices.

items.title: Poverty and exclusion: Changed-task check
items.prompt: A segregated residential zone is distant from employers, lacks transit, and has few ties to hiring networks. Which explanation best follows?
options: Relative poverty: resources fall below social norms
Absolute poverty: basic needs cannot be secured
No listed pattern: neither resource nor access gap
Social exclusion: participation is blocked by isolation
items.directions: Select the best-supported option from the four choices.

items.title: Poverty and exclusion: Repair the near-use function
items.prompt: After missing the poverty contrast, which question should be asked first?
options: Can the household secure basic necessities such as food and shelter?
Is the neighborhood isolated from institutions and social networks?
Do group health outcomes differ across the observed populations?
Does one person change rank within a career or across generations?
items.directions: Select the best-supported option from the four choices.

items.title: Poverty and exclusion: Fresh near-use re-entry
items.prompt: A household secures food and housing but cannot afford the transportation and clothing expected for routine work participation locally. Which classification fits best?
options: Absolute poverty: basic needs cannot be secured
Relative poverty: resources fall below social norms
Social exclusion: participation is blocked by isolation
No listed pattern: neither resource nor access gap
items.directions: Select the best-supported option from the four choices.

items.title: Poverty and exclusion: Repair the changed-task function
items.prompt: After missing an exclusion item, which chain should be reconstructed?
options: Low rank to occupational change to a mobility classification
Basic-needs loss to threshold calculation to policy selection
Segregation or isolation to blocked access to reduced participation
Care access difference to outcome difference to a causal conclusion
items.directions: Select the best-supported option from the four choices.

items.title: Poverty and exclusion: Fresh changed-task re-entry
items.prompt: People in a linguistically isolated community receive few public notices in accessible languages and participate less in local services. Which explanation is best supported?
options: Relative poverty: resources fall below social norms
Absolute poverty: basic needs cannot be secured
No listed pattern: neither resource nor access gap
Social exclusion: participation is blocked by isolation
items.directions: Select the best-supported option from the four choices.

items.title: Health disparities: Starting check
items.prompt: A population table shows that one income group has a higher rate of uncontrolled asthma. Which classification is most direct?
options: Health disparity: group health outcomes differ
Health-care disparity: access or delivery differs
Both disparity types: care and outcomes both differ
Neither type: no group-patterned difference appears
items.directions: Select the best-supported option from the four choices.

items.title: Health disparities: Choose with support
items.prompt: One racial group waits longer for the same clinic appointment type, while no outcome data are given. Which classification fits?
options: Health disparity: group health outcomes differ
Health-care disparity: access or delivery differs
Neither type: no group-patterned difference appears
Both disparity types: care and outcomes both differ
items.directions: Select the best-supported option from the four choices.

items.title: Health disparities: Choose with less support
items.prompt: A report shows both fewer offered follow-up visits and higher complication rates for one gender group. Which classification is supported?
options: Health-care disparity: access or delivery differs
Neither type: no group-patterned difference appears
Both disparity types: care and outcomes both differ
Health disparity: group health outcomes differ
items.directions: Select the best-supported option from the four choices.

items.title: Health disparities: Choose independently

options: Health disparity: group health outcomes differ
Both disparity types: care and outcomes both differ
Neither type: no group-patterned difference appears
Health-care disparity: access or delivery differs
items.directions: Select the best-supported option from the four choices.

items.title: Health disparities: Changed-task check
items.prompt: One racial group has fewer available primary-care appointments and a higher hospitalization rate. What classification is supported without adding causality?
options: Health disparity: group health outcomes differ
Both disparity types: care and outcomes both differ
Health-care disparity: access or delivery differs

items.title: Health disparities: Repair the near-use function
items.prompt: After missing a disparity classification, which first question repairs the function?
options: Did the person move across generations or within one career?
Are basic needs unmet or merely below prevailing social norms?
Does the measure record health status or access and delivery of care?
Do institutional records stabilize a shared social category?
items.directions: Select the best-supported option from the four choices.

items.title: Health disparities: Fresh near-use re-entry
items.prompt: A population study reports a higher prevalence of chronic pain in one gender group and no care measure. Which classification is most direct?
options: Health-care disparity: access or delivery differs
Neither type: no group-patterned difference appears
Both disparity types: care and outcomes both differ
Health disparity: group health outcomes differ
items.directions: Select the best-supported option from the four choices.

items.title: Health disparities: Repair the changed-task function
items.prompt: After missing a paired-measure item, which procedure repairs the exact function?
options: Sort each measure as care process or health outcome, then report both
Combine every measure into one disparity label before reading units
Infer that any access difference caused every reported outcome
Replace group-patterned observations with individual clinical judgments
items.directions: Select the best-supported option from the four choices.

items.title: Health disparities: Fresh changed-task re-entry
items.prompt: One income group has lower screening availability and a higher late-diagnosis rate. What classification is supported without a causal claim?
options: Health disparity: group health outcomes differ
Both disparity types: care and outcomes both differ
Health-care disparity: access or delivery differs
Neither type: no group-patterned difference appears
items.directions: Select the best-supported option from the four choices.
